title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Blocker Was the Engine, Not Aerodynamics
dek: Concorde wasn't banned because the technology failed; it was banned because the sonic boom hit the ground. Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom up into the sky, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers first to generate power.
why: The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting into data center power generation, with concrete numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.
who: Founders and investors watching hard-tech startups, aviation and data center energy — especially anyone who wants to see how a hardware company uses another market to feed its main business.
skip: The first 0:00-4:10 is launch-event-style setup and a promo video; skip to 5:12 for the actual conversation.

points.h: Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
points.body: Boom's answer to the sonic boom isn't making the aircraft quiet — it's using the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls it boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff. The boom is still generated at the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. The trick works below Mach 1.3, which is 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York and a 9:30 a.m. arrival in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean nobody is listening, so full speed is fine. Pushed to its logical extreme, it comes down to this: if there's no sonic boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

points.h: From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
points.body: The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be reversed by the next person, so he turned to pushing legislation through Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is the only way to get vote counts like that. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations and whose cycles are measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

points.h: Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
points.body: Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, the split with Rolls-Royce was public, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch themselves — and not just design it, but manufacture the hardest parts, like turbine blades, in-house. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at full power for long periods at Mach 1.7 temperatures, with the front fan removed and a generator bolted on the back, is a power generation device.

points.h: The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
points.body: Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Take off the fan, put a generator on the back, drop it into a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake pointed out specifically that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, the target is multiple gigawatts a year, and more than 10 gigawatts onto the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner ever gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it's selling to the buyer that currently has the most money.

points.h: Run on the ground first, then fly
points.body: There's an engineering side effect to Boom putting its engine into ground power first: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run enormous hours on the ground before ever being installed on an aircraft and flown. Blake admits plenty of hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation onto the ground and into data center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, actual ticket prices probably higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, can't give a firm date, and only commits to delivering at the earliest moment physically possible — from the outside that looks like around 2030. There's a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it's unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

points.h: Data center demand is so big they'll auction it
points.body: Asked whether the data center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine fires up next month, and then they plan to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is the anomalous supply-demand signal it gives: for a power product that isn't in mass production yet, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has gone from a quote to an auction.

points.h: Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Thursday
points.body: Blake recapped how fast this regulatory push moved: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, tweeted, Elon retweeted, flew to Washington that night to start lobbying for legalization, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday an aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow, though he concedes another administration would be slower. His verdict on this administration: ‘I love how fast it moves’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how one technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.
